title: sleep
hook: a king keeps asking what a person's light is, after the sun, the moon and the fire are gone

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep as a homecoming: gone to his own, and the mind settling in the breath like a bird at its peg. Did the mind land on a breath last night? Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

What light does a person have? A king named Janaka puts that to the sage Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and the answers come one at a time. The sun, Yajnavalkya says: by its light a person sits, goes out, works and comes home. And when the sun has set? The moon. And when the moon has set too? Fire. And when the fire goes out? Speech: in the dark, a person goes toward a voice. And when speech goes quiet as well? Then, Yajnavalkya says, the self is his light. Today, the dream.
screen: `WHAT LIGHT DOES A PERSON HAVE?` → `SUN, MOON, FIRE, SPEECH.` → `AND WHEN ALL OF THEM ARE GONE?`

segments.voice: Why does the conversation go there? Because Yajnavalkya is about to talk about dreaming, and dreaming is the proof. Close your eyes at night and there's no sun, no lamp, no voice. And yet a whole world shows up. Streets. Faces. A house you've never lived in that is somehow your house. What's lighting it? The text's answer, in paraphrase: in the dream, the person becomes his own light. The Sanskrit is svayam jyotih, self-lit. Then comes a passage worth hearing slowly. In paraphrase: there are no chariots there, no horses, no roads. But he makes chariots, horses and roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures. But he makes joys and pleasures. There are no ponds, no lotus pools, no rivers. But he makes ponds, lotus pools and rivers. For he is a maker. So what is the passage after? First, the dream as evidence. Yajnavalkya isn't interested in what a dream means. This isn't a dream dictionary. He's pointing at the fact that dreams happen at all, that something keeps seeing when every outer light is off. Second, the dreamer as maker. Every road in the dream was built that night, by the one asleep. Third, the turn back to waking. If something in a person can light a whole world in the dark, then the same light is there at noon, too, quietly doing the seeing behind the eyes. That's where Yajnavalkya is steering his king. And one honest note: this is the Upanishad's teaching about the self, not a claim about how the brain dreams. It asks a person to notice something, not to accept a theory.
screen: `NO SUN, NO LAMP, AND YET A WORLD` · `SVAYAM JYOTIH: SELF-LIT` · `NO CHARIOTS, BUT HE MAKES THEM` · `THE SAME LIGHT AT NOON`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the light behind closed eyes. Sit comfortably, and close the eyes. No light is coming in now, or very little. And still, things appear. A color. A face. A room from this morning. Let them come and go, without following any of them. Then turn, gently, toward whatever is seeing them. Don't try to find it. Just rest in the fact that the seeing hasn't stopped. Come back to the breath whenever you drift. If you pray, you can rest in prayer there. The bell holds the time.
Sleep. In the Brihadaranyaka, the dreamer becomes self-lit, svayam jyotih, and makes chariots, roads and rivers where there are none. Today's word.

Your line: sleep. Tomorrow morning, before you reach for the phone, stay with one dream image, or with the dark, and notice that something in you was seeing it. Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers read Yajnavalkya's teaching on the dream as a pointer to the self as the light of awareness, and study the waking, dreaming and deep-sleep states together.

fork.setup: you're Janaka. the sun has set, the moon has set, the fire is out and no one is speaking. what light does a person have now?
options: none: he sits in the dark.
fork.reveal: the self is his light, Yajnavalkya says. then he talks about dreams, where a person sees a whole world with no outer light at all.

original.note: Sanskrit svayam jyotih: self-lit. Yajnavalkya's word for the person in the dream.

trapdoor: what you thought: dreams are noise the brain makes overnight.
what it means: for Yajnavalkya, dreaming shows a light in a person that sees with every outer light gone.
what a scholar hears: svayam jyotih, and a list of chariots, roads, joys and rivers that are not there, made by the one asleep.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.2–6 (Janaka asks what light a person has: sun, moon, fire, speech, the self)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.9–10 (in dream the person is self-lit; no chariots, roads, joys or rivers there, but he makes them, for he is a maker)

notes: Brihadaranyaka 4.3.2–6: confirm the sequence (sun, moon, fire, speech, self) and the paraphrase 'sits, goes out, works and comes home' for 4.3.2.
4.3.9–10: confirm 'svayam jyotih' and the chariots/horses (rathayoga)/roads, joys, ponds/lotus pools/rivers list, and 'for he is a maker' (sa hi karta).
The lesson says plainly the passage is a teaching about the self, not a claim about the brain (science seat).
